plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple three-dimensional drawing of two conducting spheres joined by a wire. A large shaded sphere occupies the upper right of the frame, and a much smaller sphere in the same style sits at the lower left, roughly a third of the diameter of the first. Both are drawn with a soft interior highlight and are ringed by plus signs spaced around their surfaces to indicate positive charge. A thin grey curve sags gently between them, running from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small one and standing for the connecting wire. Each sphere carries a black dot at its center with a short arrow drawn from that dot out to the surface: the arrow in the large sphere is labeled 'R1' and points up and to the right, while the one in the small sphere is labeled 'R2' and points down and to the left. Giving the two spheres markedly different radii while charging both positively is what sets up the comparison. The arrangement, held at a common potential by the wire, is used to relate the surface charge density on each sphere to its radius.

elements: Large conducting sphere (radius R1) in the upper right, shaded lavender-blue with a soft off-centre interior highlight
Small conducting sphere (radius R2) in the lower left, same shading style but paler/greyer, roughly one third the diameter of the large sphere
Ring of '+' signs distributed around the visible surface of the large sphere (evenly spaced, sitting just outside the silhouette)
Ring of '+' signs distributed around the visible surface of the small sphere
Black dot marking the centre of each sphere
Radius arrow inside the large sphere: from its centre dot up-and-to-the-right to the surface, labelled 'R₁' in italic serif
Radius arrow inside the small sphere: from its centre dot down-and-to-the-left to the surface, labelled 'R₂' in italic serif
Thin grey connecting wire: a gently sagging curve from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small sphere
Potential readout labels near each sphere (V₁, V₂) showing the common or separate potentials
Surface charge density readout (σ) for the selected sphere
Highlight ring / glow applied to whichever sphere is clicked

interactions.label: Radius ratio R₁ / R₂
interactions.teaches: At a common potential the charge divides as Q ∝ R, so the smaller sphere ends up with fewer total charges but a much denser crowding of '+' signs on its surface — surface charge density goes as 1/R.

interactions.label: Connecting wire
interactions.teaches: Only the conducting wire forces V₁ = V₂ and lets charge flow until the potentials match; disconnected, each sphere keeps whatever charge it has and the two potentials differ.
Clicking a sphere highlights its radius arrow and shows its Q, V and σ, making the R-versus-σ comparison between the two conductors explicit.
The charges live on the full 3D surface of each conductor, not on a flat ring — rotating shows the '+' signs wrapping around both spheres.

demo_steps.title: Equal spheres, connected
demo_steps.narration: With R₁ = R₂ the wire equalizes the potentials and each sphere carries the same charge and the same surface charge density — the '+' signs are equally spaced on both.

demo_steps.title: The figure as drawn: R₁ = 3R₂
demo_steps.narration: Grow the large sphere to three times the small one. The wire keeps V₁ = V₂, so Q ∝ R: the big sphere holds three times the charge, yet its '+' signs are spread thinly while the small sphere's are crowded three times as densely.

demo_steps.title: Push the ratio further
demo_steps.narration: At R₁ = 6R₂ the contrast is extreme — the small sphere's surface charge density (and therefore its surface field) is six times that of the large sphere, which is why sharp, small-radius points discharge first.

demo_steps.title: Cut the wire
demo_steps.narration: Remove the wire and the spheres are isolated: charge can no longer flow, the potentials are free to differ, and the distribution frozen on each conductor no longer obeys V₁ = V₂.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: large sphere centre at (+2.2, +0.5, 0) with base radius R₁ = 1.0 unit; small sphere centre at (-2.6, -0.9, 0) with R₂ = R₁ / ratio (default ratio 3 → R₂ ≈ 0.33). Slider changes R₂ (keep R₁ fixed at 1.0) so the frame stays stable; scene spans roughly x ∈ [-3.3, 3.4], y ∈ [-1.6, 1.7]. Wire: a sagging quadratic/catenary curve in the z=0 plane from the left edge of the large sphere (≈(1.25, 0.35, 0)) to the upper-right edge of the small sphere (≈(-2.35, -0.72, 0)), dipping ~0.25 units below the straight chord; tube radius ~0.015, colour #8a8a8a. Sphere material: radial gradient highlight up-and-left of centre, large sphere #f2f4fb core → #9aa6d4 rim (lavender-blue), small sphere #fafafa core → #bfbfc6 rim (neutral grey); both slightly translucent/matte, no specular hotspot. '+' signs: flat black glyphs (stroke ~0.03 units, arm length ~0.09 for the large sphere, scaled to ~0.07 on the small one), placed just outside the silhouette and around the visible surface at radius 1.02R, always billboarded to face the camera. Number of plus signs ∝ total charge Q ∝ R: 14 on the large sphere at R₁ = 1.0, and round(14 · R₂/R₁) with a minimum of 4 on the small sphere — so at ratio 3 the small sphere shows ~5, spread over a circumference 3× smaller, i.e. 3× the linear crowding. Physics: connected ⇒ V₁ = V₂ = kQ_total/(R₁+R₂) with Q_i ∝ R_i; σ_i = Q_i/(4πR_i²) ∝ 1/R_i, so σ_small/σ_large = R₁/R₂ = slider value. Display σ in arbitrary units normalized to σ_large = 1. Radius arrows: black, head length ~0.08; large sphere's arrow points up-right at ≈ +35° from horizontal with label 'R₁' set just below-right of the shaft midpoint; small sphere's arrow points down-left at ≈ -125° (i.e. down and to the left) with label 'R₂' just above-left of its shaft. Centre dots: black spheres of radius 0.035 (large) and 0.02 (small). Potential labels V₁, V₂ in small dark-grey italic text above each sphere.
interactionPlan.notes: Render spheres as THREE.Mesh with a custom fake-gradient shader or MeshBasicMaterial + a radial-gradient canvas texture mapped so the highlight sits up-left — matching the flat textbook airbrush look rather than physical lighting. Plus signs and R-labels as CanvasTexture sprites (always camera-facing) so they stay crisp while orbiting; regenerate/reposition them whenever radiusRatio changes. Wire as a TubeGeometry along a CatmullRom/QuadraticBezier curve; when the toggle is set to 'Separated', animate the wire fading out and splitting at midpoint, and fade the shared-V label into two independent V₁ ≠ V₂ readouts. Redistribution on ratio change should tween plus-sign positions (lerp over ~300 ms) so the learner sees charge flow rather than a jump. Click picking via Raycaster on the two sphere meshes; selected sphere gets an emissive rim (thin outline mesh at 1.03R) and its radius arrow thickens, while the other dims to ~50% opacity. Keep background white and use orthographic-feeling low FOV (~28°) so the two spheres read at true relative size.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for radius ratio R1/R2: the learner changes the relative sphere sizes, the plus signs redistribute more densely on the smaller sphere while the wire keeps both at one potential, showing the inverse relationship between radius and surface charge density.
- Toggle between common-potential and separated-spheres views: the learner connects or disconnects the wire, the potential labels equalize only when connected and the charge pattern updates, making clear what the conducting wire enforces.

discrepancies: The R₁ radius arrow is drawn inside the opaque large sphere and is therefore occluded — only the italic 'R₁' label floats near the centre with no visible arrow, whereas the source clearly shows a black arrow from the centre dot to the surface.
A bright orange halo ring encircles the large sphere (selection affordance) that has no counterpart in the source and dominates the silhouette, changing the figure's colour impression.
The non-selected sphere is rendered at 50% opacity, so the small grey sphere looks washed-out/translucent instead of the solid shaded ball in the source.
Extra numeric annotations (V₁ = 0.750, σ₁ = 1.00, V₂, σ₂, 'V₁ = V₂ (wire)') are added around both spheres; they are rendered very small and clutter the clean source composition.
The centre dot and radius arrow of the small sphere are visible but the arrow direction/label offset puts 'R₂' almost on the sphere edge rather than beside the arrow shaft as in the source.
The control-panel slider caption wraps awkwardly ('Radius ratio R / 1 /R / 2 = 3.0' on separate lines), reducing readability of the main parameter control.
evaluation.notes: Composition, sphere shading, '+' charge rings and curved wire closely reproduce the source with rich, pedagogically sound interactions (ratio slider, wire connect/cut, sphere selection, guided steps), but the R₁ radius arrow is hidden inside the opaque sphere, an unrequested orange selection halo and faded non-selected sphere alter the look, and the added V/σ readout labels are too small to read comfortably.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual structure and interactions are correct; the issues are execution-level rendering fixes (occluded R₁ arrow, orange halo, faded sphere opacity, tiny cluttered readouts, slider caption wrapping).

plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 24: Electric Potential
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a simple three-dimensional drawing of two conducting spheres joined by a wire. A large shaded sphere occupies the upper right of the frame, and a much smaller sphere in the same style sits at the lower left, roughly a third of the diameter of the first. Both are drawn with a soft interior highlight and are ringed by plus signs spaced around their surfaces to indicate positive charge. A thin grey curve sags gently between them, running from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small one and standing for the connecting wire. Each sphere carries a black dot at its center with a short arrow drawn from that dot out to the surface: the arrow in the large sphere is labeled 'R1' and points up and to the right, while the one in the small sphere is labeled 'R2' and points down and to the left. Giving the two spheres markedly different radii while charging both positively is what sets up the comparison. The arrangement, held at a common potential by the wire, is used to relate the surface charge density on each sphere to its radius.

elements: Large conducting sphere (radius R1) in the upper right, shaded lavender-blue with a soft off-centre interior highlight
Small conducting sphere (radius R2) in the lower left, same shading style but paler/greyer, roughly one third the diameter of the large sphere
Ring of '+' signs distributed around the visible surface of the large sphere (evenly spaced, sitting just outside the silhouette)
Ring of '+' signs distributed around the visible surface of the small sphere
Black dot marking the centre of each sphere
Radius arrow inside the large sphere: from its centre dot up-and-to-the-right to the surface, labelled 'R₁' in italic serif
Radius arrow inside the small sphere: from its centre dot down-and-to-the-left to the surface, labelled 'R₂' in italic serif
Thin grey connecting wire: a gently sagging curve from the left side of the large sphere down to the right side of the small sphere
Potential readout labels near each sphere (V₁, V₂) showing the common or separate potentials
Surface charge density readout (σ) for the selected sphere
Highlight ring / glow applied to whichever sphere is clicked

interactions.label: Radius ratio R₁ / R₂
interactions.teaches: At a common potential the charge divides as Q ∝ R, so the smaller sphere ends up with fewer total charges but a much denser crowding of '+' signs on its surface — surface charge density goes as 1/R.

interactions.label: Connecting wire
interactions.teaches: Only the conducting wire forces V₁ = V₂ and lets charge flow until the potentials match; disconnected, each sphere keeps whatever charge it has and the two potentials differ.
Clicking a sphere highlights its radius arrow and shows its Q, V and σ, making the R-versus-σ comparison between the two conductors explicit.
The charges live on the full 3D surface of each conductor, not on a flat ring — rotating shows the '+' signs wrapping around both spheres.

demo_steps.title: Equal spheres, connected
demo_steps.narration: With R₁ = R₂ the wire equalizes the potentials and each sphere carries the same charge and the same surface charge density — the '+' signs are equally spaced on both.

demo_steps.title: The figure as drawn: R₁ = 3R₂
demo_steps.narration: Grow the large sphere to three times the small one. The wire keeps V₁ = V₂, so Q ∝ R: the big sphere holds three times the charge, yet its '+' signs are spread thinly while the small sphere's are crowded three times as densely.

demo_steps.title: Push the ratio further
demo_steps.narration: At R₁ = 6R₂ the contrast is extreme — the small sphere's surface charge density (and therefore its surface field) is six times that of the large sphere, which is why sharp, small-radius points discharge first.

demo_steps.title: Cut the wire
demo_steps.narration: Remove the wire and the spheres are isolated: charge can no longer flow, the potentials are free to differ, and the distribution frozen on each conductor no longer obeys V₁ = V₂.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World scale: large sphere centre at (+2.2, +0.5, 0) with base radius R₁ = 1.0 unit; small sphere centre at (-2.6, -0.9, 0) with R₂ = R₁ / ratio (default ratio 3 → R₂ ≈ 0.33). Slider changes R₂ (keep R₁ fixed at 1.0) so the frame stays stable; scene spans roughly x ∈ [-3.3, 3.4], y ∈ [-1.6, 1.7]. Wire: a sagging quadratic/catenary curve in the z=0 plane from the left edge of the large sphere (≈(1.25, 0.35, 0)) to the upper-right edge of the small sphere (≈(-2.35, -0.72, 0)), dipping ~0.25 units below the straight chord; tube radius ~0.015, colour #8a8a8a. Sphere material: radial gradient highlight up-and-left of centre, large sphere #f2f4fb core → #9aa6d4 rim (lavender-blue), small sphere #fafafa core → #bfbfc6 rim (neutral grey); both slightly translucent/matte, no specular hotspot. '+' signs: flat black glyphs (stroke ~0.03 units, arm length ~0.09 for the large sphere, scaled to ~0.07 on the small one), placed just outside the silhouette and around the visible surface at radius 1.02R, always billboarded to face the camera. Number of plus signs ∝ total charge Q ∝ R: 14 on the large sphere at R₁ = 1.0, and round(14 · R₂/R₁) with a minimum of 4 on the small sphere — so at ratio 3 the small sphere shows ~5, spread over a circumference 3× smaller, i.e. 3× the linear crowding. Physics: connected ⇒ V₁ = V₂ = kQ_total/(R₁+R₂) with Q_i ∝ R_i; σ_i = Q_i/(4πR_i²) ∝ 1/R_i, so σ_small/σ_large = R₁/R₂ = slider value. Display σ in arbitrary units normalized to σ_large = 1. Radius arrows: black, head length ~0.08; large sphere's arrow points up-right at ≈ +35° from horizontal with label 'R₁' set just below-right of the shaft midpoint; small sphere's arrow points down-left at ≈ -125° (i.e. down and to the left) with label 'R₂' just above-left of its shaft. Centre dots: black spheres of radius 0.035 (large) and 0.02 (small). Potential labels V₁, V₂ in small dark-grey italic text above each sphere.
interactionPlan.notes: Render spheres as THREE.Mesh with a custom fake-gradient shader or MeshBasicMaterial + a radial-gradient canvas texture mapped so the highlight sits up-left — matching the flat textbook airbrush look rather than physical lighting. Plus signs and R-labels as CanvasTexture sprites (always camera-facing) so they stay crisp while orbiting; regenerate/reposition them whenever radiusRatio changes. Wire as a TubeGeometry along a CatmullRom/QuadraticBezier curve; when the toggle is set to 'Separated', animate the wire fading out and splitting at midpoint, and fade the shared-V label into two independent V₁ ≠ V₂ readouts. Redistribution on ratio change should tween plus-sign positions (lerp over ~300 ms) so the learner sees charge flow rather than a jump. Click picking via Raycaster on the two sphere meshes; selected sphere gets an emissive rim (thin outline mesh at 1.03R) and its radius arrow thickens, while the other dims to ~50% opacity. Keep background white and use orthographic-feeling low FOV (~28°) so the two spheres read at true relative size.
